title: Lavish giving: munificence, largesse, and doing good
core: All five hover around giving on a generous scale, usually from someone who has to someone who hasn't. But they split on three separate axes: whether the word measures the **size of the gift** or the **goodness of the giver**; whether it reports an **action already taken** or merely a **kindly disposition**; and whether it stays admiring or curdles into sarcasm about the person receiving. Most are formal, most carry a faint drop in altitude from giver to recipient, and one of them is a noun — which is how the exam separates people who half-know them.
exam_note: The classic trap is **beneficent** (deed done) vs **benevolent** (intent only) — and, one step out, *beneficial*, which describes helpful things, not helpful people. Watch part of speech too: **largesse** is the only noun in the set, so a blank taking an adjective rules it out on sight.

words.nuance: The only one that is straightforwardly *praise for the size of the cheque*. It requires real wealth and a public gift — a named endowment, not a kind act — and says nothing about whether the money did any good; a **munificent** gift can be vain or useless and still earn the word.

The noun of the group: it names the handout itself, not a quality of the giver. Uniquely, it encodes the drop from giver to dependent so plainly that it usually mocks the *recipient* — "living on his father's **largesse**" — the sneer none of the adjectives here carry by default.

The only neutral, everyday word, and the only one that works as a verb (*to* **lavish** *praise on*). It measures sheer volume poured out and attaches happily to things that are not gifts at all — attention, detail, a budget — so it can indict as easily as flatter, with no implication that the giver is admirable or high-born.

The doing-good word, not the giving-money word: the benefit has already been conferred. A **beneficent** act can involve no cash whatever — a reform, a pardon, a policy — where *munificent* is unusable without money on the table.

Pure disposition: the one word here that survives a giver who has never actually given anything. A **benevolent** patron wishes you well; a beneficent one has already paid. That gap is exactly what makes *benevolent dictator* and *benevolent employer* sound so quietly sardonic.
